name: Prefect
summary: A Python workflow orchestrator where a pipeline is an ordinary function decorated with `@flow`, with retries, caching, schedules and a UI added around it.
intro: In Prefect you decorate Python functions with `@flow` and `@task`. A flow is the workflow; tasks are the steps inside it, each with its own retries, timeouts and caching. There is no separate DAG file: loops, `if` statements and calls happen at run time as in any Python program, and Prefect records each flow run and task run as it moves through states such as Scheduled, Running, Completed, Failed or Crashed. `.submit()` and `.map()` run tasks concurrently, and a cache key built from a task’s inputs, its code and the flow run lets a retried flow skip steps that already succeeded. Prefect 3 made events and automations open source, so a flow can start in response to an event, and assets track what flows produce.

To run on a schedule or remotely, a flow becomes a deployment. The simplest way is `flow.serve()`, a long-running Python process that runs the flow on a cron or interval. For more control, deployments go to work pools: a worker, a lightweight process you run, polls the pool and starts each flow run as a subprocess, a Docker container, a Kubernetes Job, an ECS task or a Cloud Run container. Push pools hand runs straight to ECS, Cloud Run, Azure Container Instances or Modal with no worker, and Prefect Managed pools run them on Prefect’s machines. The control plane is either a self-hosted Prefect server (API, UI and a database, SQLite by default or PostgreSQL 14.9+ in production) or Prefect Cloud, which adds SSO, role-based access and audit logs. Cloud has a free Hobby tier (2 users, 5 deployments), Starter at $100 a month and Team at $100 per user a month (checked October 9, 2026).
strengths: Pipelines are plain Python: existing functions gain retries, logging and state tracking with two decorators, and dynamic loops or branches need no DAG rewrite
Flexible execution: run in a local process with `serve`, on your own Kubernetes, Docker or ECS through workers, or on serverless push and managed pools without a worker
Events and automations are open source since 3.0, so event-driven runs and alerts don’t require Prefect Cloud
Prefect Cloud prices by users and deployments rather than per run, with your code and data staying in your own infrastructure on hybrid work pools
limits: Major versions have broken user code: Prefect 1.0 flows needed changes to run on 2.0 (2022), and 3.0 (2024) moved to Pydantic 2 and removed async tasks in sync flows
Caching across runs needs result persistence, which is off by default, so results must be stored somewhere such as S3 or GCS
Self-hosting means running the server, its database and workers yourself, and SSO, RBAC and audit logs exist only in Prefect Cloud
Prefect announced in July 2026 that it is acquiring Dagster Labs, so one company now steers two rival orchestrators; it positions Prefect for execution and Dagster for data assets

sections.title: Prefect, Dagster and Temporal
sections.intro: All three run steps and retry failures, but they start from different questions. Prefect’s own founder describes the split: Dagster’s answer was assets, Prefect’s was execution. Temporal records every step so code can resume exactly where it stopped.

notes: Prefect’s comparison pages, including Prefect vs Airflow, are the vendor’s own view.

story: Prefect was founded in 2018 by Jeremiah Lowin, when, as Lowin later wrote, “most of the world’s data work still ran on cron jobs and hand-tended DAGs”. Its open-source Python package reached PyPI in March 2019. The pitch, still on Prefect’s comparison pages, is that a pipeline should be your Python code as-is, not code restructured into DAG objects, operators and XCom messages the way Apache Airflow requires.

Prefect 2.0 left beta on July 27, 2022 after nearly a year of building in public, and it was a rewrite: Prefect 1.0 flows needed changes to run on it. Prefect 3.0 followed in September 2024 with an open-source events and automations backend, faster runtime, and caching built on transactional semantics. On July 13, 2026, Lowin announced that Prefect was acquiring Dagster Labs, its rival since both were founded in 2018. Prefect says Dagster and Dagster+ continue, and describes the split as Dagster defining outcomes, Prefect executing the work and FastMCP, its third product family, governing access for AI agents.

choices.choice: Workflows as ordinary Python, not a declared DAG
choices.why: Tasks are created as the code runs, so a flow can loop over data or branch on a result without describing the graph up front, which Prefect presents as its main difference from Airflow’s static DAGs.
Prefect Cloud or a Prefect server tracks state and schedules, while workers and push pools run the code in the user’s own infrastructure, so data doesn’t have to pass through Prefect.
Workers replaced the older agents during Prefect 2 and are standard in Prefect 3. A pool’s type (Kubernetes, Docker, ECS and so on) decides how each run’s infrastructure is created.
Cache keys hash a task’s inputs, code and run, so retrying a pipeline reuses results that already succeeded instead of redoing their side effects.
